leo.name: Low Earth Orbit
leo.description: Close to Earth (~400 km). Quick orbits, cheap launch, easy to reach.
leo.why: Low radiation and high data rates. Best for Earth observation and beginner missions.

ssorbit.name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit
ssorbit.coverage: Global, same local time every pass
ssorbit.description: Polar orbit where the satellite passes over the same spot at the same local time each day.
ssorbit.why: Consistent lighting — ideal for climate and wildfire monitoring.

meo.name: Medium Earth Orbit
meo.description: Used by GPS/navigation satellites. Higher radiation (Van Allen belts).
meo.why: Good coverage but more radiation and lower data rate than LEO.

geo.name: Geostationary Orbit (GEO)
geo.description: Stays over one point on the equator. Needs a big launcher and lots of delta-v.
geo.why: Constant view of one region, but expensive to reach and weaker data link.

lunar.name: Lunar Orbit
lunar.description: Orbiting the Moon. Long eclipses (two-week night) and high delta-v.
lunar.why: Far from Earth: weaker signal, longer delay, needs more power for night.

lagrange.name: L1 / L2 Lagrange Point
lagrange.description: A gravitationally stable point a million km away (JWST is at L2). Great for telescopes.
lagrange.why: Very stable, far from Earth interference, but hard to reach and service.

heliocentric.name: Mars Transfer / Heliocentric
heliocentric.description: An orbit around the Sun, en route to or at Mars. The hardest destination.
heliocentric.why: Long delay, high radiation, weak signal — advanced missions only.

molniya.name: HEO / Molniya
molniya.description: Highly elliptical orbit that dwells over high latitudes (Russia/Canada).
molniya.why: Good polar coverage, but passes through intense radiation belts.
